entries.name: Bread wheat
entries.wild_ancestor: wild emmer and goatgrass (Aegilops tauschii) hybrids
entries.spread: across Eurasia by 5000 BCE; now grown on every continent
entries.notes: The world's default grain and the game's existing wheat_0..7 growth stages. Bread wheat is the staff of life; half of humanity's daily calories once ran through it.

entries.name: Common rice
entries.spread: southern and eastern Asia, then worldwide by the Columbian exchange
entries.notes: Feeds more people per hectare than any cereal. Flooded paddy is a distinct landscape block set: bunded water, standing water, green arcs.

entries.name: Maize (corn)
entries.spread: the Americas by 1500 BCE; Europe, Africa and Asia after 1492
entries.notes: Teosinte to 12-row ears in a few thousand years: the most dramatic single act of plant domestication. Tall stalks read well as a 1-2 block crop.

entries.name: Barley
entries.spread: one of the first crops; the staple of Egypt, Mesopotamia and medieval northern Europe
entries.notes: The highest-altitude and highest-latitude cereal on Earth; grows in Tibet and above the Arctic Circle. The old north's bread grain; malting feeds the beer supply.

entries.name: Sorghum (great millet, guinea corn)
entries.spread: across Africa, then India and China along trade routes; America after 1700s
entries.notes: The champion of semi-arid heat: tillers like a little cane and shrugs off drought. Feed, thatch and syrup as well as grain.

entries.name: Oats

domesticated.where: Europe, as a weed of barley fields

entries.spread: northern Europe; the horse-fodder and porridge grain of the medieval Atlantic fringe
entries.notes: A secondary domesticate: it began as the weed people stopped weeding. The western maritime grain; porridge, oatcake and fodder.

entries.name: Rye

domesticated.where: Fertile Crescent, then a cold-grain of northern Europe

entries.spread: central and eastern Europe; the black bread staple from Poland to Russia
entries.notes: The grain of the cold, poor, sour north: survives frosts that kill wheat. Dark dense loaf; also rye whiskey and rye grass for pasture.

entries.name: Emmer wheat
entries.spread: Europe, Egypt, India by 5000 BCE
entries.notes: One of the founder crops. Hulled grain: the husk stays on, so threshing needs a dehusking step. Survives as a heritage crop for rustic breads and farro.

entries.name: Einkorn wheat
entries.spread: across the Near East with early farming; largely replaced by emmer and bread wheat
entries.notes: The oldest domesticated wheat and the smallest grain. A living relic: founder-crop status, tiny plots, nutty flour for specialty baking.

entries.name: Durum wheat (pasta wheat)
entries.wild_ancestor: domesticated emmer derived (Triticum turgidum ssp. durum)
entries.spread: the Mediterranean basin by 3000 BCE; the pasta and couscous grain
entries.notes: Hard amber grain with high gluten: semolina for pasta and couscous. Distinctive awned ears; the wheat of the dry Mediterranean rim.

entries.name: Spelt
entries.spread: Bronze Age Europe; a niche health-grain today
entries.notes: A hulled hexaploid relative of bread wheat; the medieval German and Swiss staple. Hardy in cold wet uplands where bread wheat fails.

entries.name: Khorasan wheat (Kamut)
entries.spread: Egypt and the Near East; revived as the trademarked 'Kamut'
entries.notes: A giant-grain heirloom, twice the kernel of bread wheat. Bolted straight from Egyptian tomb legend into modern health-food marketing.

entries.name: Triticale
entries.wild_ancestor: human-made bread wheat x rye hybrid
entries.spread: worldwide forage and fodder cereal since the 1960s
entries.notes: The one cereal we invented outright: wheat's kernel, rye's toughness. Mostly stockfeed and silage rather than human bread.

entries.name: Pearl millet (bajra, bulrush millet)
entries.wild_ancestor: wild pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum ssp. monodii)
entries.spread: the Sahel and India; the fourth most important cereal in its dryland zone
entries.notes: Grows where almost nothing else will: hot sand, half a metre of rain. Fat, finger-like seed heads; staple roti of Rajasthan.

entries.name: Foxtail millet (Italian millet, xiaomi)
entries.spread: China and Korea, then Europe (Romania to Italy) via the steppe
entries.notes: One of China's oldest grains and the dynasty staple before rice took the south. Small round bristly heads like a fox's tail.

entries.name: Proso millet (broomcorn millet)
entries.wild_ancestor: wild proso millet (Panicum miliaceum ssp. ruderale)
entries.spread: Eurasia and India; a quick catch-crop across the steppes
entries.notes: The 60-day cereal: a summer rescue crop when the main one fails. Birdseed ancestry (it's the millet sprayed for parrots).

entries.name: Finger millet (ragi, dagussa)
entries.spread: east and southern Africa, and southern India (ragi)
entries.notes: Hand-shaped seed heads like fingers; the grain stores for a decade without rotting, making it the famine crop of Ethiopia and India.

entries.name: Teff
entries.spread: Ethiopia and Eritrea; tiny-grain health food in the west
entries.notes: The smallest grain in the world: a thousand teff seeds weigh less than a gram. The sole source of injera flatbread.

entries.name: Fonio (hungry rice)
entries.spread: the Sahel belt from Senegal to Sudan
entries.notes: The quickest cereal alive: ripe six weeks after sowing, so it feeds people in the hunger gap before the big harvest.

entries.name: Little millet
entries.spread: India, especially the dry Deccan
entries.notes: One of India's ancient minor millets, drought-proof and famine-proof. Tiny grain for porridges and rotis of the dry zone.

entries.name: Kodo millet
entries.spread: India, chiefest among the ancient south Indian millets
entries.notes: The most resilient of India's sacred millets; survives almost total drought. Grain and leaf-fodder both valuable.

entries.name: Barnyard millet (sanwa)
entries.spread: India and Japan / Korea (as 'hie')
entries.notes: A weed tamed: barnyard grass became a crop across two continents. Eaten during fasting days in India; a typhoon crop in Japan.

entries.name: African rice
entries.spread: West African rainforest and savanna fringe; mostly displaced by Asian rice
entries.notes: Africa's own rice, domesticated twice on Earth. Tougher against local diseases than Asian rice; a conservation priority for fragile tropics.

entries.name: Job's tears (adlay, coix)
entries.spread: tropical Asia; ornamental beads worldwide from the hard shiny shell
entries.notes: The grain with a built-in necklace: each seed sits in a polished pearly bead used for rosaries. Glutinous adlay is a Filipino holiday grain.

entries.name: Canary seed
entries.spread: Mediterranean basin; the world's birdseed crop
entries.notes: Grown almost entirely to feed caged birds; now a niche gluten-free human food ('kanary' porridge in the Canary Islands).

entries.name: Wild rice (manoomin)

domesticated.where: North America, modern cultivation in Minnesota / California

entries.spread: Great Lakes region; paddy-grown in North America since the 1950s
entries.notes: Not a rice and barely domesticated: seeds still shatter at ripeness. Harvested by canoe by Ojibwe nations for centuries; a gourmet long-grain.

entries.name: Quinoa
entries.spread: the Andean altiplano; the fashionable 'supergrain' of the 2000s
entries.notes: The Inca's sacred grain, iron-rich and complete-protein. Not a grass at all: a goosefoot, cousin of fat hen and spinach.

entries.name: Grain amaranth
entries.spread: Aztec Mexico and Inca Peru; rediscovered in the 1970s as a health grain
entries.notes: The Aztec imperial grain, nearly extinguished after the conquest (Spanish banned it over ritual uses). Popped like popcorn; tiny black seed.

entries.name: Buckwheat
entries.spread: across Eurasia; the blini, soba and kasha grain
entries.notes: A rhubarb relative whose seeds are ground for soba and blini. Bees work it; one of the last nectar flows of autumn.

entries.name: Tartary buckwheat
entries.spread: the Himalayan arc and Yunnan; the 'bitter buckwheat' of high Asia
entries.notes: Hardier and more bitter than common buckwheat, stuffed with rutin. The mountain grain of Tibet and Yunnan; leaves and grain both bitter.
